modalLead: The biggest release since 1.0, and a long run of work: nineteen changes across a hundred and fourteen files. All of it is about one thing — the life of a link. How it gets in from wherever you are, how you find out it has rotted, how the tidying becomes something you can finish in two minutes, and how a page you saved tells you it has something new. The dashboard also arrives about five times lighter.

items.text: Save from your phone's share sheet. Install nextDash as an app and it appears wherever you share a link — the link lands in the Inbox and nextDash opens on it. Android sometimes hands over the address inside the text rather than as a link; it is picked out either way.

And from any browser, with a bookmarklet. Config → Help → Inbox builds one for you, carrying this install's own address — so it works in Safari, Firefox and everywhere else the extension will never reach. On an install with a password, capture gets a key of its own that opens nothing else.

Ready-made pieces for the launcher you already use. A shell script, two Raycast commands, a Dropzone action, a Ulauncher extension, and recipes for Alfred and Apple Shortcuts — all saving through the same one-line route.

A link you already have is found wherever it is. The check used to look only at the page you were saving to, so the same link filed on Work went straight in again from Personal. Saving a second copy on one page is refused, as before; a copy on another page is a question — “You already saved this on Work · Docs”, with the existing bookmark one click away and Save anyway if you meant it.

sections.title: Links rot, and now you can watch it happen

items.text: A broken link says how long it has been broken. Failing for three weeks is a different problem from failing since this morning, and the list now tells them apart — on the row, in the filters and in the export.
A page that answers 200 while saying “not found” is caught. The polite kind of disappearance — a shop that removed the product, a docs site that swallowed a page — used to read as perfectly healthy.
One host down reads as one problem. Group the list by site and forty rows from the same server stop looking like forty separate emergencies.

A dead link can be pointed at its last archived copy, with the original address kept in the note — the capture is a reading of the page, not the page, and the address is where a later attempt to find it again starts.

Rot report in the toolbar answers the once-a-month question: what has gone, what has moved or been rewritten, what has been failing for over a month, what is broken and was never opened, and what broke this week. The list is the work queue; this is the read.

Ten links, two minutes. When enough links want attention, a card in the corner names what is waiting — “10 links to review: 4 broken, 3 never opened, 3 not opened in a year” — and starts a session over the worst ten, one card at a time.

The session ends. It says how many you actually dealt with, offers another ten while more are waiting, and Done for today puts the offer away until tomorrow. Skipping is not handling, so the count at the end is honest — and a number that never ends is a number people learn to ignore.

sections.title: What changed while you were away

items.text: Fresh. When a page you saved offers a feed, the bookmark can carry a small count of what it has published since you last opened it, and a Fresh collection lists those bookmarks newest first. Every other collection keys on what you did; this one keys on what changed, which is the one question they cannot answer.
Opening the bookmark clears it, and that is the whole of it. No article list, no read state to keep in order — this is not a feed reader, only a bookmark that can say 3.

Filter the page you are on with Shift + F: a slim bar narrows the rows in place, hides the categories left empty, and keeps the layout, the cursor and any selection. Search still takes you anywhere; this stays here.
You come back where you were. A long page is a place you are somewhere in. Switching pages, dipping into Health or config, even a reload — you land at the offset you left.
A selection can be pinned and set to a checking mode in one action, and a bulk tag change can be taken back. A mixed selection pins rather than flipping each row into the opposite of its neighbour.
Move a bookmark to the category beside it with Shift + Alt + ← / →, without opening anything.

A shortcut opens the moment it matches again — and we should not have changed that. v1.2.0 made Enter the default because an instant shortcut can swallow an ordinary word that starts with the same letters. That does happen, and it is the rare case; what the change did was charge every shortcut a second keystroke on every use to prevent it, which is most of the reason to have a shortcut gone. The default is back, and existing dashboards are moved with it. Both other ways are still under Behavior → Search: open after a short pause, or press Enter — and a shortcut that keeps eating a word you type can also just be renamed.

The printable cheat sheet carries every shortcut. It was one A4 with a curated selection, so a key could be in the app and not on the paper. It now runs to as many pages as the app has keys — the live sheet behind ! is unchanged.

Find a setting by what it is set to. “Which one is on 8099”, “what did I set to Monitor” — the question you have when something behaves oddly and you cannot name the setting. The value is matched and shown beside the location.

The settings that do not follow the device rule say so. With Keep settings on this device only on, a handful stay shared by design — those carry an all devices mark, because they are the ones that surprise you on the other machine.
Duplicate a page or a category, with or without the bookmarks in it. Copies start with a clean check history, since a copied uptime would be a claim about a link this copy has never checked.

Edit a name or a shortcut where you read it. Double-click the title, or click the shortcut pill — including the faint + on a bookmark that has none. A key already in use is named as you type it and refused, rather than quietly breaking the bookmark that had it.

The dashboard arrives in one piece. First load went from 169 requests and 915 KB to 30 requests and 685 KB — same page, same files, served as bundles, with each view's styles arriving when you open that view.
Config opens quicker and weighs less. A cold open is about a third faster, and the bookmark list draws a third fewer elements — most noticeable on a long list and a slow machine.
